newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Airlift of refugees from Zaire passes 10,000 mark.
newsitem.headline: Airlift of refugees from Zaire passes 10,000 mark.

text.p: The number of Rwandan Hutu refugees flown home from Zaire passed the 10,000 mark on Wednesday but aid officials say tens of thousands others would probably miss the U.N. airlift because they are missing or dead.
Nearly 1,500 refugees left aboard six flights by mid-afternoon on Wednesday, pushing to over 10,000 the total repatriated since the airlift began in earnest on April 27.
But a spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said the organisation had dramatically scaled down its estimate of how many would eventually take this route home.
"We now think we will probably only move around 40,000 refugees back to Rwanda by air," said UNHCR spokesman Peter Kessler. "The rest are either missing or dead."

The United Nations had hoped to airlift over 80,000 refugees encamped about 40 km (25 miles) south of the northeast Zairean city of Kisangani, but all of them fled their camps after attacks by local villagers and Zairean rebel soldiers.

Around 40,000 of them have since drifted back to the camps, many of them with horrendous machete, axe and bullet wounds from the attacks. They said that in the dense forests surrounding their camps hundreds had died of wounds, of hunger or disease.
At Biaro camp on Wednesday, over 70 corpses were lying by the side of the road awaiting burial in mass graves which local Red Cross workers are digging. They had all died overnight.
Thousands of skeletal refugees were lining the entrance to the camp, waiting for the daily aid convoy that on Wednesday was again delayed and frustrated by bureaucracy.
Kessler said rebel soldiers held up Wednesday's convoy from Kisangani for over three hours on the grounds that it needed permission from the governor to travel.

A climate of suspicion and mistrust continues to sour the relationship between aid workers and officials of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, the rebel force which has captured about three quarters of Zaire since launching its offensive in October.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has promised aid agencies free access to all areas under his control but U.N. officials still cannot go more than 41 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani.
"The cooperation is insufficient," said Kessler. "Every day we are inching forward but we are not able to make the strides neccessary to do the job properly."
Aid officials said they had heard reports that thousands of refugees from Biaro had been killed at kilometre 52 on the dusty road. They said they were still trying to confirm the reports.

The refugees, remnants of more than a million Hutus who fled to Zaire in 1994 to escape reprisals for the genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus, fled deeper into the country when the Tutsi-dominated rebels launched the offensive.
One group of 80,000 trekked more than 500 km (300 miles) through dense forest to near Kisangani, Zaire's third city.
